items.title: Three linear equations, three different endings
items.prompt: Linear equations do not all end with a number. Work these three and say, each time, what kind of equation you were given.

parts.label: a

expect.form: as a value of $x$ or a solution set

hints: Simplify each side completely before you move anything across.
The minus sign in front of $(x-7)$ multiplies both terms: $-x+7$.
Left side $6x-11$, right side $4x+7$.

solution.text: Distribute on the left, and distribute the leading minus on the right.
Both sides are now linear.
Subtract $4x$, add $11$, divide by $2$.
1 mark for correct distribution on both sides (the minus in front of the bracket is where this is lost); 1 mark for collecting to a correct linear equation; 1 mark for $x=9$ stated as a solution.

parts.label: b
hints: The LCD of 2, 5 and 10 is 10.
Multiply **every** term by 10 — including the $\tfrac1{10}$ on the right.
Keep each numerator in brackets: $-2(x+3)$, not $-2x+3$.

solution.text: Multiply every term on both sides by the LCD, 10.
The bracket on the subtracted fraction matters.
1 mark for multiplying every term by 10 (a term missed here loses the whole question); 1 mark for the bracketed expansion; 1 mark for $x=4$.

parts.label: c

options: Conditional — it has exactly one solution
An identity — every real number is a solution
A contradiction — it has no solution

hints: Simplify the left side and compare it with the right.
If the variable disappears, look at what is left: is it true or false?

solution.text: Distributing the 2 gives exactly the right-hand side.
Every $x$ cancels and leaves a true statement, so every real number satisfies the equation.
It is an **identity**; the solution set is all real numbers, $(-\infty,\infty)$.
1 mark for the simplification; 1 mark for naming it an identity **and** stating that the solution set is all real numbers — the name alone is half the answer.

items.title: A rational equation whose only candidate is forbidden
items.prompt: Consider $$\frac{x}{x+4}+3=\frac{-4}{x+4}.$$ Work through it in the order the mark scheme expects: restrictions first, algebra second, verdict last.

parts.label: a
hints: A denominator may never be zero.
Solve $x+4=0$ and exclude what you get.

solution.step: Find the zero of the denominator

solution.text: The restriction is $x\ne-4$, and it is written down **before** any solving.
1 mark. Writing the restriction after solving earns nothing on this paper — the whole point is that it is known in advance.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What is the LCD of the equation?
hints: There is only one distinct denominator here.
The constant 3 counts as $\tfrac{3}{1}$, which needs no new factor.

solution.text: 1 mark. A wrong LCD makes everything after it wrong, so it is marked on its own.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Multiply through by the LCD and solve. What is the candidate?
hints: Multiplying gives $x+3(x+4)=-4$.
Expand the bracket before collecting.

solution.text: 1 mark for multiplying all three terms; 1 mark for reaching $x=-4$. Note the word *candidate*: nothing has been solved yet.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Give the solution set of the original equation.
hints: Compare the candidate with the restriction from part (a).
A value excluded at the start cannot become a solution at the end.

solution.text: The only candidate is $x=-4$, which is exactly the excluded value.
$x=-4$ is **extraneous**. The equation has no solution.
Multiplying by $x+4$ multiplied both sides by zero at $x=-4$, and multiplying by zero makes any two things equal.
1 mark for rejecting the candidate against the restriction; 1 mark for writing the answer as *no solution* or $\{\ \}$. A bare $x=-4$ scores zero for the question, however clean the algebra above it.

items.title: Five places an imaginary unit can appear
items.prompt: Write each expression in standard form $a+bi$. Give exact values; no decimals.

parts.label: a
hints: Convert each radical to $i$ form **before** you multiply.

solution.text: The product rule $\sqrt a\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}$ needs non-negative radicands, so it may not be used here.
$\sqrt{144}=12$ is the trap: it has the right digits and the wrong sign.
1 mark for converting both radicals before multiplying; 1 mark for $-12$. The answer $12$ scores zero — it is the whole point of the question.

parts.label: b
hints: The powers of $i$ repeat every four.
Divide 43 by 4 and keep the remainder.

solution.text: 1 mark for using the cycle of four; 1 mark for $-i$.

parts.label: c
hints: Expand as you would any two brackets.
Then replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$ — that term becomes real.

solution.text: 1 mark for a correct expansion; 1 mark for replacing $i^{2}=-1$; 1 mark for the collected standard form.

parts.label: d
hints: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, $2+i$.
The denominator becomes $2^{2}+1^{2}$.

solution.text: $(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^{2}+b^{2}$, always real.
Standard form means two separate parts, not one fraction.
1 mark for using the conjugate; 1 mark for a correct numerator; 1 mark for splitting into real and imaginary parts. Leaving $\frac{-1+7i}{5}$ loses the last mark on a paper that says *standard form*.

parts.label: e
hints: First write $\sqrt{-72}$ in $i$ form and simplify the radical.
$\sqrt{-72}=i\sqrt{72}=6i\sqrt2$.
Then divide **both** terms by 4.

solution.text: This is where marks go: the 4 divides the $-10$ as well.
1 mark for $6i\sqrt2$ (radical simplified, not left as $\sqrt{72}$); 1 mark for dividing both terms by 4; 1 mark for the simplified standard form.

items.title: One quadratic, seen four ways
items.prompt: Take $2x^{2}-5x-3=0$. Every part below is a different route to the same pair of numbers — which is the point.

parts.label: a

expect.form: as a product of two brackets

hints: Look for two numbers multiplying to $2\cdot(-3)=-6$ and adding to $-5$.
Those are $-6$ and $+1$: split the middle term as $2x^{2}-6x+x-3$.

solution.text: $ac=-6$ and the two numbers are $-6$ and $+1$.
1 mark for a correct split or trial factorisation; 1 mark for the product. Multiply back to check — an unchecked factorisation is a guess.

parts.label: b
hints: Set each factor equal to zero.
$2x+1=0$ gives a fraction, not $-1$.

solution.text: 1 mark for setting each factor to zero; 1 mark for both values, written as a solution set.

parts.label: c
hints: $a=2$, $b=-5$, $c=-3$ — carry the signs.

solution.text: 1 mark for the signed substitution — losing the sign of $c$ turns $+24$ into $-24$ and the verdict with it; 1 mark for 49.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: What does that discriminant tell you?

options: Two distinct real solutions, and they are rational
Two distinct real solutions, both irrational

hints: Positive, zero or negative decides the *kind* of solutions.
49 is also a perfect square. What does that add?

solution.text: $\Delta=49>0$, so there are two distinct real solutions.
$49=7^{2}$, and with integer coefficients that means the roots are **rational** and the quadratic factors — which part (a) had already shown.
1 mark for two distinct real solutions; the perfect-square observation is what lets you skip the formula next time.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Completing the square turns the equation into $(x-h)^{2}=k$. Write that equation.
hints: Divide through by 2 first, then move the constant across.
$x^{2}-\tfrac52x=\tfrac32$. Half of $\tfrac52$ is $\tfrac54$.
Add $\left(\tfrac54\right)^{2}=\tfrac{25}{16}$ to **both** sides.

solution.text: Half the $x$-coefficient, squared, added to both sides.
$x-\tfrac54=\pm\tfrac74$ gives $x=3$ and $x=-\tfrac12$, the same pair as part (b).
1 mark for dividing by 2 before completing the square; 1 mark for adding the square to both sides; 1 mark for the final form. This is the exact skill chapter 3 reuses for vertex form.
1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How many solutions, and of what kind?
hints: A negative discriminant means the square root is of a negative number.
Nonreal roots of a real quadratic always come in pairs.

solution.text: $\Delta<0$, so the radical is imaginary.

solution.step: Say it in the course's words
solution.text: **Two nonreal solutions** — a conjugate pair. Not "no solutions": there are two, they are simply not real.
1 mark. The answer "no solution" scores zero here; that phrase belongs to an equation with no roots at all.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give both solutions in standard form.
hints: $x=\dfrac{4\pm6i}{2}$ — then divide **both** terms by 2.

solution.text: 1 mark for $6i$; 1 mark for dividing both terms by 2 (halving only the real part is the standard slip); 1 mark for the conjugate pair.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: What is the sum of the two solutions?
hints: Add them and watch the imaginary parts.
Also: for $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ the sum of the roots is $-b/a$.

solution.text: Conjugates cancel their imaginary parts, which is exactly why a real quadratic cannot have just one nonreal root.
1 mark. The observation that the sum is real is the reason nonreal roots arrive in pairs — worth remembering for chapter 3.

items.title: A right triangle out of a sentence
items.prompt: In a right triangle the longer leg is $2$ cm more than twice the shorter leg, and the hypotenuse is $1$ cm more than the longer leg. Build the model, then solve it.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Let $s$ be the shorter leg in centimetres. Write the longer leg in terms of $s$.
hints: "Twice the shorter leg" is $2s$.
"2 more than" adds 2 to the whole of that.

solution.text: Twice the shorter leg, then two more.
1 mark. Writing $2(s+2)$ instead — adding before doubling — is the usual error and it changes the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the equation the triangle satisfies.
hints: The hypotenuse is 1 more than the longer leg, so it is $2s+3$.
Pythagoras puts the two legs on one side and the hypotenuse alone on the other.
Every term is squared.

solution.text: One more than the longer leg.
Legs on the left, hypotenuse on the right.
1 mark for the hypotenuse expression; 1 mark for putting the hypotenuse alone on one side — swapping it with a leg is the mistake this part is testing.

parts.label: c
hints: Expand all three squares before collecting.
The $s^{2}$ terms partly cancel, leaving $s^{2}-4s-5=0$.

solution.text: $s$ was defined as a length, so $s=-1$ is impossible: $s=5$ cm.
1 mark for correct expansion; 1 mark for the quadratic; 1 mark for both roots; 1 mark for rejecting the negative root **with a reason**.

parts.label: d
hints: Substitute $s=5$ into $s$, $2s+2$ and $2s+3$.
Check with Pythagoras before you write the answer down.

solution.text: The sides are 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm.
1 mark for all three lengths with units; the Pythagorean check costs ten seconds and catches an arithmetic slip in the expansion above.

items.title: A ball thrown from a roof
items.prompt: An object moving vertically under gravity has height $s=-\tfrac12gt^{2}+v_{0}t+s_{0}$, with $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}$. A ball is thrown straight up at $14.7$ m/s from a roof $19.6$ m above the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the model for the height $s$ (in metres) after $t$ seconds.

expect.form: as an equation for $s$ in terms of $t$

hints: $v_{0}$ is the initial velocity and $s_{0}$ the initial height.

solution.text: 1 mark for $-4.9$ (the half and the minus sign together); 1 mark for putting $v_{0}$ and $s_{0}$ in the right places.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: At what time does the ball hit the ground?
hints: "Hits the ground" means $s=0$.
Divide the whole equation by $-4.9$ to make it easy: $t^{2}-3t-4=0$.
That factors.

solution.text: Dividing by $-4.9$ clears every decimal at once.
Time runs forward from the throw, so $t=4$ s.
1 mark for setting $s=0$; 1 mark for solving; 1 mark for choosing the positive root with a reason. Dividing by $-4.9$ first is not required but is where the arithmetic marks are usually saved.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which root did you discard, and why?
hints: Look at the root you did not use.
What would a negative time mean here?

solution.text: A negative time is one second **before** the ball was thrown, when the model does not apply. It solves the equation and not the situation.
1 mark for naming the root; the reason is what the question is really asking for, and "it is negative" alone is a weaker answer than "it is before the throw".

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: How high is the ball after 1 second?
hints: Substitute $t=1$ into the model.

solution.text: Higher than the roof, as it should be one second into an upward throw.
1 mark, with the unit. An answer of $-4.9+14.7+19.6$ left unevaluated is not an answer.

items.title: Four machines in a row
items.prompt: Each part is a different kind of equation. Name the machine to yourself before you start — that decision is what the exam is testing.

parts.label: a
hints: Isolate the absolute value before splitting.
$\lvert 2x-3\rvert=5$.
Two cases: $2x-3=5$ and $2x-3=-5$.

solution.text: 1 mark for isolating before splitting; 1 mark for both cases; 1 mark for both values. Splitting before isolating gives $2x-3=\pm20$ and two wrong answers.

parts.label: b
hints: $\lvert u\rvert=\lvert w\rvert$ means $u=w$ or $u=-w$.
Negate the **whole** of $x-6$: $-(x-6)=-x+6$.
Two linear equations, one solution each.

solution.text: The bracket is the whole point.
1 mark for writing both cases; 1 mark for negating the entire right-hand side; 1 mark for both solutions.

parts.label: c
hints: Square both sides, then bring everything to one side.
The candidates are 10 and 2 — now check them.

solution.text: $x=2$: left $\sqrt9=3$, right $-3$. ✗  $x=10$: left $\sqrt{25}=5$, right $5$. ✓
1 mark for squaring correctly; 1 mark for both candidates; 1 mark for the check that rejects $x=2$. An unchecked pair of answers loses the last mark even though both numbers are on the page.

parts.label: d
hints: One exponent is twice the other, so substitute $u=w^{1/3}$.
Cube each $u$ to get back to $w$ — and a cube root of a negative number is fine.

solution.text: Cube both, since $w=u^{3}$.
1 mark for spotting the quadratic form and substituting; 1 mark for both $u$ values; 1 mark for cubing back. Stopping at $u$ answers a different question and scores nothing for the last mark.

parts.label: e
hints: Each $u$ gives an $x^{2}$, and each $x^{2}$ gives **two** values of $x$.

solution.text: Do not lose the $\pm$.
1 mark for the substitution; 1 mark for both $u$ values; 1 mark for all **four** values of $x$. A fourth-degree equation has four roots, and answering with two is the error this part exists to catch.

items.title: Two radicals, and a check that keeps both roots

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Rearrange so that one radical stands alone. Write that equation.

expect.form: as an equation with one radical isolated

hints: Squaring a difference of two radicals leaves a cross term worse than the original.
Move the second radical to the right-hand side.

solution.text: Squaring now leaves only **one** radical on the right, instead of a product of two.
1 mark. Squaring the equation as given is not wrong, only much longer, and it is where the arithmetic errors happen.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Square once and simplify. Write the equation you get.

expect.form: as an equation with the radical alone on one side

hints: The left side is just $2x+9$.
Collect the non-radical terms: $2x+9-x-5=x+4$.

solution.text: 1 mark for expanding the square with its middle term (forgetting $2\cdot2\cdot\sqrt{x+1}$ is the classic slip); 1 mark for isolating the remaining radical.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Square again and give both candidates.
hints: Everything to one side gives $x^{2}-8x=0$ — factor, do not divide.

solution.text: Dividing by $x$ here would delete the root $x=0$.
1 mark for the second squaring; 1 mark for factoring rather than dividing by $x$; 1 mark for both candidates.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Check both in the original equation. Which survive?
hints: Substitute $x=0$: $\sqrt9-\sqrt1$.
Substitute $x=8$: $\sqrt{25}-\sqrt9$.
Squaring *can* create extraneous roots. It does not always.

solution.text: Both survive; the solution set is $\{0,8\}$.
Checking is not a ritual for finding a root to throw away — it is how you learn which candidates are solutions. Sometimes the answer is all of them.
1 mark for substituting both into the **original** equation (not into a squared version); 1 mark for the solution set.

sections.title: Linear, Compound, and Absolute Value Inequalities

items.title: One inequality, three notations
items.prompt: Solve $$\frac{2x-1}{3}-\frac{x+2}{2}\ge-\frac{5}{6}$$ and present the answer the way the paper asks for it: graphed, in set-builder notation, and in interval notation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Multiply through by the LCD. Write the resulting inequality.

expect.form: as an inequality with no fractions

hints: The LCD of 3, 2 and 6 is 6.
6 is positive, so nothing flips at this step.
Keep each numerator in brackets.

solution.text: The multiplier is positive, so the symbol is unchanged. This is the step where a negative multiplier would flip it.
1 mark for the correct multiplication with brackets kept; 1 mark for leaving the symbol alone, which is only creditable because you can say why.

parts.label: b
hints: Expand: $4x-2-3x-6\ge-5$.
Collect: $x-8\ge-5$.

solution.text: 1 mark for the expansion; 1 mark for $x\ge3$ with the symbol the right way round.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the solution set in set-builder notation.
hints: The form is $\{x\mid\text{condition}\}$.
Read it aloud: "the set of all $x$ such that $x$ is at least 3".

solution.text: 1 mark. The vertical bar (or a colon) reads "such that" and is not optional.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Write the solution set in interval notation.
hints: $x\ge3$ includes 3, so that end is a square bracket.
The other end is infinite.
$\infty$ never takes a square bracket.

solution.text: $\ge$ includes the endpoint, so a square bracket.
Unbounded above, and infinity is not a number that can be included.
1 mark, and it is all or nothing: $[3,\infty]$ is marked wrong on this paper.

parts.label: e

options: An open circle at 3, shaded to the right
A closed circle at 3, shaded to the right
A closed circle at 3, shaded to the left
An open circle at 3, shaded to the left

hints: $\ge$ includes the endpoint.
Which direction do the values go?

solution.text: $x\ge3$ contains 3 itself, so the circle at 3 is filled in.
Every number bigger than 3 also works, so shade to the right.
1 mark for a closed circle; 1 mark for shading to the right. An open circle on a $\ge$ is the same error as a round bracket in part (d) — and the two are marked separately, so it costs twice.

items.title: Absolute value inequalities, including the two with no boundary point
items.prompt: Give every answer in interval notation. Two of these four have no boundary points at all — recognising which is the exercise.

parts.label: a
hints: Isolate: $\lvert x+3\rvert\le3$.
A less-than becomes a single sandwich: $-3\le x+3\le3$.
Subtract 3 from all three parts.

solution.text: 1 mark for isolating; 1 mark for the three-part form; 1 mark for the interval with **closed** ends, since the inequality is $\le$.

parts.label: b
hints: A greater-than splits into two cases joined by **or**.
Both cases divide by $-3$, so both symbols flip.

solution.text: Dividing by $-3$ reverses the symbol.
Two rays, joined with $\cup$, both ends open.
1 mark for splitting into two cases rather than a sandwich; 1 mark for flipping in **both** cases; 1 mark for the union with open ends.

parts.label: c

expect.form: as an interval or the empty set

hints: Isolate the absolute value first and look at what it must be less than.
$\lvert 2x-7\rvert<-5$.
How small can an absolute value get?

solution.text: An absolute value is a distance, so it is never negative — it cannot be less than $-5$.
No solution: $\varnothing$.
1 mark for isolating; 1 mark for the empty set with the reason. Splitting into $5<2x-7<-5$ and grinding out an "answer" scores zero.

parts.label: d
hints: Divide by $-2$ — and remember what that does to the symbol.
$\lvert x-1\rvert>-3$.
How small can an absolute value get?

solution.text: Dividing by a negative reverses the symbol, before anything is split.
Every absolute value is at least 0, and 0 already beats $-3$. Every real number works.

1 mark for the flip; 1 mark for recognising that the inequality is automatically true and writing $(-\infty,\infty)$. This part and part (c) are the pair the lecture slides never state, and both have appeared on papers.
